newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodian orphans caught in political wrangle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodian orphans caught in political wrangle.

text.p: The orphans at this former military barracks are too young to understand the recent coup in Phnom Penh, but they appear to grasp what it means to be on the losing side in Cambodian politics.
Armed soldiers have angrily accused them of harbouring Khmer Rouge guerrillas in their dormitories.
The older boys have been threatened with guns and told they must leave with government troops. And the younger children have watched soldiers take away their toys, clothes, shoes and medicine.
Now government troops have informed them they must leave their home as the facility will again be turned into a military barracks, the children and orphanage directors say.

The dormitories are said to be slated to house forces of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6 after accusing the prince of illegally bringing Khmer Rouge rebels into the city.
"Soldiers came yesterday and told me the air force would come to stay here," orphanage director Soth Mel said earlier this week.
Children said soldiers, who visit them nearly every day, told them that if they did not leave, armed forces would attack their orphanage and destroy all the buildings.

Staff said they have appealed to co-Defence Minister Tea Banh and other high-ranking government officials to allow them to stay and have received assurances from Tea Banh that the orphans would be protected.
But when contacted for comment, Tea Banh said he knew nothing about the orphanage. Another official, General Mol Reup, denied plans to oust the orphans.
The conflicting reports are not uncommon in Cambodia these days, where Hun Sen's new regime is striving for credibility as reports of human rights abuses and intimidation continue to plague him.

Soth Mel and the 40 children he cares for at the Rasmei Sobhanna Orphanage are caught in the middle, and it has not helped that their local benefactors are from Ranariddh's inner circle -- a fact they say is not lost on the new government.

Ranariddh's wife, Princess Marie, helped set up the orphanage. Australian Geraldine Cox, the only member of Ranariddh's cabinet who has not left the country, helps to run daily operations and funds the facility through contributions from Australian nationals and a private foundation.
"If the Cambodian People's Party wants this place, they'll take it," she said of Hun Sen's party. "They'll take the orphans and we won't be able to help anymore."

The orphanage's history is no less controversial. The barracks there used to house the personal forces of Prince Norodom Chakrapong, Ranariddh's brother, a member of Hun Sen's party who was exiled for allegedly attempting to overthrow Hun Sen in 1994.
After Chakrapong was exiled, Ranariddh turned the site into an orphanage in a move that orphanage staff acknowledge may not have been entirely legal.
The children, who huddle together in their dormitories or an open-air dining room instead of playing, understand little of the political manoeuvres. They only know they are afraid.
"The soldiers came to the orphanage, and threatened me, asking if there were Khmer Rouge in the centre. We said there were no Khmer Rouge, we are only orphans," said one 14-year-old boy.
"They thought I was a soldier because I had short hair, but I begged them not to take me. They said we would have to leave the orphanage because we were hiding the enemy," he added.

"They took my toy dog, guitar, watch," said another boy, who shifted his weight from foot to foot, barely raising his eyes. "They took the clock off the wall, the clothes, our shoes. They took also took 30 chickens from our farm."
Sy Kosal, a 19-year-old who grew up at the orphanage, had been out on his own, working as an assistant at the headquarters of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party until the July 5-6 fighting.
Now he, too, is caught in politics and back at the orphanage. In too much pain to talk, he lay in a bed at his old dormitory recovering from shrapnel wounds incurred during the recent fighting.
